title: Valorization of Agro-Industrial Residues for Bioethanol: A Comparative Review of Brewer’s Spent Grain, Cassava, and Yam Peels
content:
Escalating global energy demand and the environmental consequences of fossil fuel
dependence have intensified the need for renewable energy sources. Bioethanol
derived from lignocellulosic biomass represents a promising alternative. This
review critically evaluates the valorization of three agro-industrial
residues—yam peels, cassava peels, and brewer’s spent grain (BSG)—for bioethanol
production, focusing on the interplay between feedstock composition, pretreatment
efficiency, and process optimization. A central finding of this analysis is
that the significant variability in reported ethanol yields is directly
attributable to the inherent heterogeneity in the proximate and chemical
composition of the feedstocks, compounded by disparities in pretreatment
methodologies and saccharification protocols. Pretreatment plays a crucial role
in breaking down the resistant lignocellulosic structure, thereby enhancing the
enzymatic hydrolyzability of cellulose and hemicellulose. Optimal conversion
efficiency is strongly correlated with feedstocks possessing high carbohydrate
and low inhibitory compound profiles. Of the residues examined, BSG
demonstrates the highest suitability as a fermentation substrate with
documented ethanol yields surpassing 70% and, in optimized processes, approaching
94%. Advanced statistical optimization and modeling techniques have proven
instrumental in enhancing conversion kinetics, reducing operational costs, and
improving the techno-economic feasibility. This waste-to-energy paradigm contributes
to energy security and exemplifies circular economy principles by converting
low-value waste streams into high-value biofuel, thereby addressing challenges
in waste management and climate change mitigation. The review concludes by
delineating persistent challenges and future research trajectories,
underscoring the necessity for integrated technological innovations to realize
the full potential of sustainable, lignocellulosic bioethanol production.
